title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
hook: love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know: Tirumular's short verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kannappa, the hunter who knew none of the rules, was stopped by Shiva's own hand.

Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. That's the first line of a short Tamil verse, spoken by a man the tradition calls Tirumular. How he got that name is strange. A traveling yogi comes upon a herd of cows gathered around the body of their cowherd, who has just died. The cows are lowing, circling, refusing to leave him. The yogi can't bear it. So, the story says, he leaves his own body and enters the cowherd's. And the cowherd stands up.
screen: `COWS AROUND A DEAD COWHERD.` → `A YOGI CAN'T BEAR IT.` → `THE COWHERD STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest, as the Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The cows, comforted, go home. The yogi means to return to his own body, but when he looks for it, it's gone. Shiva's will, the story says. So he stays in the cowherd's body, under the cowherd's name, Mular, and settles down to meditate and compose the Tirumantiram, a long book of verses on Shiva and the path to him. It sits in the Tirumurai, the collection that holds the Tevaram. Now the verse, in paraphrase. Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. No one knows that love itself is Shiva. When they know that love itself is Shiva, they rest there, as love, as Shiva. The verse doesn't say Shiva is loving, the way you'd say a person is kind. It goes further: the love is Shiva. Not a quality he has, but who he is. Now go back to the field. The story starts with a man who couldn't bear the grief of some cows. He wasn't seeking a vision. He was moved by animals crying for their herder, and gave up his own body to comfort them. Before he wrote a single verse, he'd already done what the verse says. Looking back over these Tamil days: Appar, who belonged so wholly to Shiva that a king couldn't summon him; Sambandar, whose heart was stolen; Kannappa, who held nothing back; and a cowherd who was really a yogi, saying it plainly: love itself is Shiva.
screen: `THE BODY HE COULDN'T FIND` · `THE TIRUMANTIRAM` · `LOVE ITSELF IS SHIVA` · `HE DID IT BEFORE HE WROTE IT`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, a person or even an animal, see their face for a moment, and feel the warmth that comes with it. Then gently let the face fade and stay with the warmth, not the person now, just the love; when the mind goes looking for the face, let it, and come back. If you pray, you can rest in the verse's words: love itself is Shiva.
Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, Tirumular, the yogi who entered a cowherd's body to comfort his cows, and whose verse says love itself is Shiva. Today's word.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Some cows grieved, and a yogi couldn't bear it. Tomorrow we travel north and east, to Bengal.

howItsDone: Tirumular is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and the words 'anbe sivam', love is Shiva, from his verse are spoken and written by Tamil Shaivas.

chat.says: What does Tirumular mean when he says love itself is Shiva?
options: Not that Shiva is loving, like a kind person; the love is Shiva, who he is.
That Shiva loves only those who give up their bodies, as the yogi did.
That Shiva once fell in love with a cowherd and took his name.
chat.meaning: The verse goes past 'Shiva is loving': those who know that love itself is Shiva rest there, as love, as Shiva.

Tirumular.meaning: the yogi-poet who lived on in a cowherd's body

Mular.meaning: the cowherd's name, which the yogi kept

yogi.meaning: someone who practices yoga, a disciplined seeker

Tirumurai.meaning: the sacred collection of Tamil Shaiva hymns

notes: Editor pass: the writer's draft retold Sundarar's interrupted wedding and the 'madman' hymn, already told on day 1371. Rewritten as a new angle on the same index line: Tirumular and the 'anbe sivam' verse. New practice and carry; the look-back now names this run's figures (Appar, Sambandar, Kannappa, Tirumular).
The verse number varies by edition (often given as 270); the script cites it by first line only. Confirm paraphrase.

The traditional claim that he wrote one verse a year over thousands of years is deliberately left out under the claims rule. The yogi's origin (Kailasa, Sundaranatha) and the village (Sattanur) are left unnamed.
The Tirumantiram is the tenth Tirumurai, not part of the Tevaram (1–7); the script says only 'in the Tirumurai, the same collection'. Confirm.
